title: SAP stops most travel and hiring because of AI's soaring cost
excerpt: Having worked at some giant firms that heavily depend on SAP, I would think their position as "system of record for procurement/production" would get stronger with AI.
content_html:
Having worked at some giant firms that heavily depend on SAP, I would think their position as "system of record for procurement/production" would get stronger with AI.

e.g. AI + a good database of what your company does seems like an excellent combination.


Or AI can be a threat: If AI can spit out good enough special purpose tools a lot of the SAP adaption business goes away. If AI then also assists in data migration the moat goes away.


EAI has existed for twenty years...Tibco, webMethods, IBM AppConnect...SAP is still what it is. How is AI going to make a dent on this?


The same argument can be made about snowflakes and other providers that handle the data layer. If they can leverage AI in a safe contained environment they would become the clear winner


LOL

Although they may internally use LLM, I wanna say said they were not going to allow their core offering to be integrated with LLM

Although maybe they reversed course?


Would a technology famous for hallucinating data often enough, and in many context unable to guarantee it won't assume and hallucinate when it feels "confident enough" despite a robust system prompt, be really considered for a "system of record for procurement/production" usage?

(yes yes RAG exists)


In the ERP space, AI is being used mostly for repetitive tasks, documentation and forecasting-type activities or where a non-deterministic answer might be useful. Scanning in documents and using OCR to create an order, asking what page I use to do X, historical demand modelling and constraint scheduling. Also have seen it used to do order flow type stuff like suggesting products to sell if they buy ABC. I'm not really seeing it being used to do heavy analysis and they've generally been careful not to put it in places where a hallucination could result in a bad business decision.


> Scanning in documents and using OCR to create an order,

I remember this being done more than 10 years ago.

The other uses cases you describe also were being done. Of course with AI maybe it’s become easier and cheaper?


Yes but it generally expected documents to be in a certain layout and the user had to fill in a lot of the gaps. It's more able to identify elements on an incoming PO, match a supplier invoice, or create a receipt based on a packing list with inference.

EDIT: The other activities, yes I think it made it cheaper and easier. They both required human intervention to make an accurate forecast or execution plan. Forecasting requires humans to do things like apply smoothing factors, identify abormal demand over huge datasets, or identify seasonal demand cycles, etc. Constraint scheduling requires a human to intervene in dispatching and resource allocation as well. AI can do 95% of the work with a proposal, or even control the process. Supposedly much better than historical algorithms. I haven't implemented this part of it, but I've seen it done.

The documentation part is much more robust. You can ask it complex questions, like "How do I setup a phantom blow-through part in a MS level 1 BoM?" and it walks you through the entire thing. With the sales suggestions, it can identify things like "The customer is buying spaghetti and pancetta" AI: "They are probably making carbonara, how about some garlic bread?"


Take your favorite OCR software.

Then take a photo of a document and throw it into ChatGPT, or Gemini, along with the word "Transcribe".

ChatGPT wins, by a landslide. BUT AI's advantage doesn't stop there.

"Take this picture of some idiot filling in form 49, I've also attached the PDF, fill in the PDF fields, provide a database record according to the schema attached and flag if there are any obvious problems with the entries".

That works too. "Produce a latex document of this kid's math homework and flag any problems" - works. "Produce a MS word document of this letter" - works. "Read this bill and produce a JSON version following the schema from this example" ... and so on and so forth.

More than that, it is starting to work pretty well with Gemma 31B local model (will still do 30 document analyses on cpu only, at Q4 on a DDR4 or higher machine. Yes it's mostly memory speed that matters) at this point. I mean, that's GPT 5.0 or so quality (95% correct with the occasional problem), but hey, Qwen 3.8 27B may be coming out next week ...


Actually 30 is sequential on an hosted Xeon server. No GPU, about 2 minutes for a ~2000 token answer. I should try parallel since you're quite right, I should be able to do faster that way.


The big risk for these platforms is that AI reduces the cost to switch to another ERP. IF AI can map all of the data between two different competitors, the whole business model is finished


Maybe but I work for a company that integrates with a lot of ERPs and I don't know why but the rando IT guy who can't get themselves out of a paper bag is still a thing. You'd think AI would help them but man ... doesn't seem like it.


That is not what ERPs are used for.

Would love to hear how AI is going to help here. This is like a young engineer thinking the CDC machine they just bought, is going to make Airbus and Boeing obsolete...


It’s well known that the moat of system of record is how difficult it is to extract your data into another system.


> It’s well known that the moat of system of record is how difficult it is to extract your data into another system.

I think that is one aspect but not the biggest issue.

The specific shape of data and shape of functionality gets built around for decades due to incompleteness of any system, expanding dependencies and changing business needs.

Decades of building around the system results in a mountain of work when trying to replace the system, typically a larger body of work than implementing the base system itself.


most of this complexity is because 1000 different types of businesses are jammed into the same database schema and ERP. Its all non sense


ERPs are often used as a lot more than a system of record: they’re directly engaged with as the LOB software point-of-contact by many expert employees, and function as a sort of encoding of organizational behavior.

They’re a lot more than a data store or system whose primary value is ingesting info and producing reports.

For a lot of business, replacing the ERP is on par with replacing Excel. It’s not about getting the data into another system; it’s about all of the complexity and expertise required to use it.


Does it? Those are big numbers, but it looks like in 2024 they sold €4b of assets to juice income for 2025.


Sounds like a paperclip maximizer to me.

Seriously, why the duck aren't they running their own AI systems in house???


TL;DR:

“Under the policy, only Al-related hiring, customer-facing travel and trips directly linked to the company's Al initiatives or mission-critical employee Al training are exempt, reflecting SAP's focus on "be disciplined in how we spend" while expanding its Al capabilities.”

no-paywall: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49222851


Wait, first they stopped hiring because AI is going to replace everybody. Now they stopped hiring because AI, which was going to replace everybody, costs too much.

You can’t make this stuff up.


This is less of an issue than the headline suggests. I worked for a publicly traded US company remotely. The company was based between Ft. Lauderdale and West Palm Beach Florida. It was a roll of the dice each spring if the CFO would pull the trigger on a travel block for about 6 weeks around spring break when flights and hotels were most expensive. Approvals were available for critical projects. It was only ever about not exceeding a quarterly budget number; nothing else.


Anecdotally, I know several companies that have given the directive of "Use more AI instead of hiring more people". I wonder whether this is part of the story here too?


If you believe that AI does add to productivity gains, say equivalent to adding 10-20% employees, would you do anything differently than SAP?


Not really. A company can work and do things without having to run RCTs to prove everything. The market itself is the RCT.


If you doubt that you have gained something as high as 20% gains, it probably just means you got nothing.

And also, individual productivity isn't the same as organisation productivity, especially at such a large company.


  > gained something as high as 20% gains

all other things being held constant, i suppose it should be as easy as +20% profit rate? tho im not an executive so what do i know...


This tells me we’re getting close to “peak bubble.” We saw these same sort of stupid headlines just before the dot-com bubble popped, too. When companies are distorting regular business to do the new thing, they’ve gone past the point of reasonableness on the new thing and we’re ready for a snap-back.


This "AI business" has really opened my eyes to how..insane the average person is, and just how bad discourse has gotten.

Look at the conversation: people are writing off this technology (on a tech forum no less) as useless, because it can make mistakes. We criticize the cost, and the business models, and the companies, the purveyors and users. Why? Because we don't quite understand how best to use it...3 years in.

People have lost all concept of time scales, I guess. They expect everything to be polished and mature NOW. How many people realize that could take a decade or more?

So, yeah, a stodgy old company has figured out they don't need to hire and don't need to travel, and AI is expensive. So what?


This kind of thinking (we'll figure it out how to use it correctly, it is awesome technology) is not new. There was blockchain psychosis (blockchain/crypto solves everything!) for a decade, which is now replaced with AI will solve everything.


NFT was surprisingly short-lived considering it rode on the coattails of the blockchain


The difference is that cryptocurrencies never had an obvious benefit beyond subverting the existing banking sector. A more apt comparison would be to cloud computing, which likewise had its host of detractors (“It’s just somebody else’s computer!”) but which brought very obvious benefits to small developers and enterprises which couldn’t host their own hardware.


"This time it's different" is also a refrain we've heard with every new bubble. It shouldn't be surprising that some people want to take a measured, skeptical approach. Even if it means they are slightly behind the bleeding edge. Even if you have to play catch-up, it can be more efficient to let others find all the dead ends first and avoid them.


What does crypto have to do with this? DuPont has sunk billions into synthetics that were looking for a business model and ultimately proved useless. Why not compare AI to that?


Is blockchain really your analogy here? Something that is also new?

You are proving my point.

You say it's "not new", but then don't seem to have any gauge of technological history. How long before the internet was monetized? 30 years?


About 30 years ago we had the sitcom bubble. Tulip mania was in the 1630ies, about 400 years ago.

There always have been attempts to exploit others for personal gain and people following that.

The new thing is the speed in which this happens globally. But there had been other accelerators bringing equal jumps. Introduction of cross ocean telegraph cables, flight, book printing, ...

True, modern technology makes results globally available with very little marginal costs.

However on the spread of ideas the last item mentioned on the list above is extremely interesting to study: Book printing brought translations of the Bible into more places and took reproduction and interpretation of those texts out of the hands of the few (mostly the church) to broader masses (for as long as people could read) which lead to lots of political conflicts and redistribution of power in Europe with impact to colonies worldwide. By people following one interpretation of a text and derived rules more than another. To a large degree since books with ideas could now be replicated within days instead of years. As now ideas are replicated within minutes rather than days.


This is reasoning from shallow similarity. If you have not been able to find areas where AI actually does solve things, I don't know what to tell you. Go look at the number of vulnerabilities being solved. Go look at the speed of their solves. On the opposite side, go look at the number of vulnerabilities being found and exploited. Go look at the speed of their being exploited. Yes, it's a negative externality, but it's an example of an extreme productivity boost, which is easy to measure. Take a minute dropping on YouTube or X and actually look for people who are making small scale manufacturing. Look at the speed of their development cycles. Not software development cycles, real world atom development cycles. And then compare it to the speed of their development as of five years ago. Notice a difference? Even the complaints of crypto, while valid, are a bit overstated given that there are hundreds of millions of people in third world countries where money transfers are not reliable, not stable, and they depend on crypto. Yes, there's a bunch of criminals as well. I agree. My point is superficial dismissal is head-in-the-sand behavior. And that's your choice. I mean, it's fine by me.


It's not useless, it's just dangerous to use. It's like heroin basically. It does make you feel good instantly, and it can be a life-saver in certain situations of extreme pain or chronic pain (cancer), but there is a reason people are prohibiting the original substance, and also trying to develop less dangerous versions, such as methadone and tramadol.


This isn’t unreasonable at all. AI has promised to cause an unprecedented, continuous disruption to the working class. “Being replaced by robots” - a topic anyone of working age is very familiar with. Why would you be surprised there exists a proportionate amount of pushback in the form of incoherent rhetoric?


What I find the most amusing is ... "AI code is crap". I think I heard enough time "this codebase is shit, we need a full rewrite" to know that no one agrees what is quality code.

Suddenly, everyone are expert writing the most elegant, clean and without bug code.


It will be interesting to see if SAP can turn into the basis for companies that use AI heavily or if companies that use AI heavily will prefer to replace SAP.

Who are the contenders that start fresh with focus on AI?

One that comes to mind is IONOS. They seem to be in the process of building something like a "SAP in the times of AI" from the ground up. Starting with the demands of SMEs. It looks like an interesting approach to me: Having a "knowledge base" for each customer, initially filled with the data from the website. Then let the customers add more data. Then offer agents that do work for the customers. Answer calls and emails and do marketing for example.


I have in mind what I think is a very strong framework to allow companies to replace legacy ERPs quickly with AI help. I guess I should get on with it and publish something!


> It will be interesting to see if SAP can turn into the basis for companies that use AI heavily or if companies that use AI heavily will prefer to replace SAP.

Considering the human and institutional complexity of implementing ERP, CRM, whatever the hell Concur is supposed to be, etc. I'd bet on most organisations implementing AI around and with those systems instead of replacing them with something vibecoded / "AI native" vendors.

blocks.html_en:
> It’s well known that the moat of system of record is how difficult it is to extract your data into another system.

I think that is one aspect but not the biggest issue.

The specific shape of data and shape of functionality gets built around for decades due to incompleteness of any system, expanding dependencies and changing business needs.

Decades of building around the system results in a mountain of work when trying to replace the system, typically a larger body of work than implementing the base system itself.

blocks.html_en:
This "AI business" has really opened my eyes to how..insane the average person is, and just how bad discourse has gotten.

Look at the conversation: people are writing off this technology (on a tech forum no less) as useless, because it can make mistakes. We criticize the cost, and the business models, and the companies, the purveyors and users. Why? Because we don't quite understand how best to use it...3 years in.

People have lost all concept of time scales, I guess. They expect everything to be polished and mature NOW. How many people realize that could take a decade or more?

So, yeah, a stodgy old company has figured out they don't need to hire and don't need to travel, and AI is expensive. So what?

blocks.html_en:
About 30 years ago we had the sitcom bubble. Tulip mania was in the 1630ies, about 400 years ago.

There always have been attempts to exploit others for personal gain and people following that.

The new thing is the speed in which this happens globally. But there had been other accelerators bringing equal jumps. Introduction of cross ocean telegraph cables, flight, book printing, ...

True, modern technology makes results globally available with very little marginal costs.

However on the spread of ideas the last item mentioned on the list above is extremely interesting to study: Book printing brought translations of the Bible into more places and took reproduction and interpretation of those texts out of the hands of the few (mostly the church) to broader masses (for as long as people could read) which lead to lots of political conflicts and redistribution of power in Europe with impact to colonies worldwide. As now ideas are replicated within minutes rather than days.

blocks.html_en: This is reasoning from shallow similarity. If you have not been able to find areas where AI actually does solve things, I don't know what to tell you. Go look at the number of vulnerabilities being solved. Go look at the speed of their solves. On the opposite side, go look at the number of vulnerabilities being found and exploited. Go look at the speed of their being exploited. Yes, it's a negative externality, but it's an example of an extreme productivity boost, which is easy to measure. Take a minute dropping on YouTube or X and actually look for people who are making small scale manufacturing. Look at the speed of their development cycles. Not software development cycles, real world atom development cycles. And then compare it to the speed of their development as of five years ago. Notice a difference? Even the complaints of crypto, while valid, are a bit overstated given that there are hundreds of millions of people in third world countries where money transfers are not reliable, not stable, and they depend on crypto. content_html_zh: 我曾在一些严重依赖 SAP 的大公司工作过，我认为他们作为“采购/生产记录系统”的地位将通过人工智能而变得更强。人工智能+一个关于您公司业务的良好数据库似乎是一个绝佳的组合。或者人工智能也可能成为一种威胁：如果人工智能能够推出足够好的专用工具，那么很多 SAP 适配业务就会消失。 如果人工智能也有助于数据迁移，那么护城河就会消失。EAI 已经存在了二十年...Tibco、webMethods、IBM AppConnect...SAP 仍然是原来的样子。 人工智能将如何对此产生影响？对于雪花和其他处理数据层的提供者也可以提出同样的论点。 如果他们能够在安全的环境中利用人工智能，他们将成为明显的赢家哈哈，虽然他们可能在内部使用法学硕士，但我想说他们不会允许他们的核心产品与法学硕士集成，尽管也许他们改变了方向？一项以经常产生幻觉数据而闻名的技术，并且在许多情况下无法保证它不会假设和幻觉，尽管有强大的系统提示，但它感觉“足够自信”，是否真的会考虑用于“采购/生产记录系统”的使用？（是的，RAG 存在）在 ERP 领域，人工智能主要用于重复性任务、文档和预测类型的活动，或者非确定性答案可能有用的地方。 扫描文档并使用 OCR 创建订单，询问我使用哪个页面来执行 X、历史需求建模和约束调度。 还看到它用来做订单流类型的事情，比如建议他们购买 ABC 时出售的产品。 我并没有真正看到它被用来进行繁重的分析，而且他们通常很小心，不把它放在幻觉可能导致糟糕的商业决策的地方。> 扫描文档并使用 OCR 创建订单，我记得这是 10 多年前完成的。您描述的其他用例也正在完成。 当然，有了人工智能，也许一切都会变得更容易、更便宜？是的，但它通常期望文档采用某种布局，并且用户必须填补很多空白。 它更能够识别传入采购订单上的元素、匹配供应商发票或根据装箱单进行推理创建收据。编辑：其他活动，是的，我认为它使它更便宜、更容易。 它们都需要人工干预来做出准确的预测或执行计划。 预测需要人类做一些事情，例如应用平滑因子、识别庞大数据集上的异常需求或识别季节性需求周期等。约束调度还需要人类干预调度和资源分配。 AI可以完成提案中95%的工作，甚至可以控制流程。 据说比历史算法要好得多。 我还没有实现这部分，但我已经看到它完成了。文档部分更加强大。 您可以向其提出复杂的问题，例如“如何在 MS 1 级 BoM 中设置虚拟吹穿零件？” 它会引导您完成整个过程。 通过销售建议，它可以识别诸如“顾客正在购买意大利面条和薄饼”之类的信息 AI：“他们可能正在制作意面，来点大蒜面包怎么样？”带上你最喜欢的 OCR 软件。然后拍一张文档照片，并将其连同“转录”一词一起扔进 ChatGPT 或 Gemini。ChatGPT 以压倒性优势获胜。 但人工智能的优势还不止于此。“拍一张某个白痴填写 49 表格的照片，我还附上了 PDF，填写 PDF 字段，根据附加的模式提供数据库记录，并标记条目是否存在任何明显问题”。这也有效。 “制作这个孩子的数学作业的乳胶文档并标记任何问题” - 有效。 “生成这封信的 MS Word 文档” - 有效。 “阅读此法案并按照此示例中的架构生成 JSON 版本”... 不仅如此，它开始与 Gemma 31B 本地模型配合得很好（第四季度仍将在 DDR4 或更高版本的机器上仅在 cpu 上进行 30 个文档分析。 是的，此时最重要的是内存速度。 我的意思是，这是 GPT 5.0 左右的质量（偶尔出现问题时正确率为 95%），但是嘿，Qwen 3.8 27B 可能会在下周发布......实际上 30 在托管 Xeon 服务器上是连续的。 没有 GPU，约 2 分钟即可得到约 2000 个令牌的答案。 我应该尝试并行，因为你是对的，这样我应该能够做得更快。这些平台面临的最大风险是人工智能降低了切换到另一个 ERP 的成本。 如果人工智能能够映射两个不同竞争对手之间的所有数据，那么整个商业模式就完成了也许吧，但我在一家集成了很多 ERP 的公司工作，我不知道为什么，但无法摆脱纸袋的随机 IT 人员仍然是一件事。 你可能会认为人工智能会帮助他们，但伙计...... 看起来不像。这不是 ERP 的用途。很想听听人工智能将如何提供帮助。 这就像一个年轻的工程师认为他们刚刚购买的 CDC 机器将使空客和波音被淘汰......众所周知，记录系统的护城河是将数据提取到另一个系统的难度。>
